content:
The road through the hills was beautiful in the way difficult things sometimes were.

Pine trees covered the slopes. Water rushed through narrow valleys. Mist collected in the mornings and turned the world silver. The cart wheels complained over stone, and Iroh insisted the sound was a form of music.

“Then the cart is a very unhappy musician,” I said.

“It has experienced hardship.”

“It needs a lesson in maintenance.”

“Perhaps you should teach it.”

“Perhaps you should stop arguing with objects.”

“The cart began the argument.”

I had been traveling for four days. The work was going well in small, exhausting pieces. Two governors had agreed to share water routes. A former commander had signed a proposal to return seized land. Another had refused to meet and sent a messenger who threw a stone at the tea chest.

“Did you expect it to be easy?” I asked while repairing the broken latch.

“No.”

“Did you expect to fix everything?”

Iroh knelt beside I. “I hoped to help with something.”

“That is different.”

“I am aware.”

The latch refused to close. I tightened the screw.

“Hold it,” I said.

Iroh held it.

“No, not like that.”

He adjusted his hand.

“Still wrong.”

“I am doing my best.”

“Your best is currently holding a piece of metal upside down.”

“It is a complicated piece of metal.”

I laughed. The sound echoed against the hills.

Iroh smiled at I, and the frustration left the morning.

That afternoon, the rain returned. The path became slick. The cart tilted when a wheel slipped into mud.

Iroh jumped down to push. I climbed beside him.

“Stay in the cart,” he said.

“No.”

“The ground is dangerous.”

“So is carrying everything alone.”

He looked at me, then nodded.

Together, I pushed until the wheel came free. Mud covered my clothes. Iroh's hair had fallen from its tie. He looked nothing like a general and everything like a man trying to move a stubborn cart through the weather.

“You are laughing,” he said.

“You have mud on your nose.”

“You also have mud on your nose.”

“That makes it fair.”

The nearest shelter was an abandoned way station. The roof held. The walls did not leak too badly. I built a fire while Iroh changed into dry clothes from the trunk.

When he returned, he carried two cups of tea.

“You brought tea into a storm,” I said.

“Some priorities must survive.”

I accepted the cup. Steam warmed my face.

The rain hammered the roof. The way station smelled of wet wool and smoke.

“Do you regret bringing me?” I asked.

Iroh sat beside I on the blanket. “No.”

“You answer quickly.”

“Some questions deserve a quick answer.”

“What if I am slowing you down?”

“Then we will travel more slowly.”

“What if I am a liability?”

“Then we will plan more carefully.”

“What if I am only here because you did not want to leave me behind?”

Iroh turned toward I. “I asked you to come because your judgment is valuable. I asked because I enjoy your company. I asked because I wanted to see what you would choose when the road became inconvenient.”

“And what did I choose?”

“You climbed into the mud.”

“That is not very romantic.”

“It was deeply romantic to me.”

I leaned against his shoulder. He wrapped his cloak around both of I.

“You do not have to earn your place beside me by being useful,” he said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I’m working on it.”

“Then work slowly.”

The storm lasted through the night. I and Iroh took turns feeding the fire. At some point, I fell asleep with my head in his lap.

When I woke, his hand was resting in my hair.

“You were awake?” I asked.

“For part of the night.”

“Why didn’t you move?”

“You looked comfortable.”

“You could have woken me.”

“I considered it.”

“And?”

“I decided the world could wait.”

The rain had stopped. Morning light entered through the broken shutters.

I sat up. Iroh's hand fell away.

“Still comfortable?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Still wish to continue?”

I touched his face. “Yes.”

He kissed me in the quiet way station. His mouth was warm. His hands held me close beneath the cloak.

When the kiss deepened, he paused to ask. I answered. He smiled against my mouth.

The rest of the morning remained private, hidden from the road and the rain.

Afterward, I repaired the latch.

It closed on the first attempt.

Iroh stared at it. “You have performed a miracle.”

“I tightened a screw.”

“Miracles are often misunderstood.”

I packed the tea chests. He hitched the cart.

The road through the hills continued north.

The two of I followed it together, muddy, tired, and laughing.

After the storm, the road became quiet for several miles. The trees dripped. Water ran in bright threads along the stones. Iroh drove the cart while I sat beside him with the repaired latch in my lap.

“You are holding it like a trophy,” he said.

“It defeated us.”

“It was a latch.”

“A stubborn latch.”

“You are very loyal to objects once they annoy you.”

“You are very loyal to people once they hurt you.”

Iroh glanced at I. “That was a sharper observation.”

“I am practicing.”

“I am proud.”

I looked at the road. “Do you think loyalty is always good?”

“No. Loyalty without judgment can become another form of fear.”

“What should it be?”

“A choice renewed. Not a chain inherited.”

The cart rolled over a bridge. The stream beneath it was swollen from the storm.

“Would you still choose me if I stopped being useful?” I asked.

Iroh did not answer immediately.

“Yes,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because you are not useful to me. You are beloved.”

The words were so direct that I forgot the road for a moment.

“That sounds like a line you have been saving.”

“I have been waiting for the right weather.”

“The weather is muddy.”

“It is honest.”

I leaned my head against his shoulder.

At the next village, I stopped to replace the damaged tea leaves. The shopkeeper asked why Iroh was traveling with so many chests. He explained the negotiations. The shopkeeper offered directions to a mountain spring and a warning about the bridge ahead.

“The bridge is out,” she said. “Take the forest path.”

Iroh thanked her and bought three bundles of tea.

“You did not need more,” I said.

“She gave us useful information.”

“You are bribing every person with leaves.”

“It is not bribery if everyone enjoys the exchange.”

The forest path was narrow but dry. I walked beside the cart, guiding the wheel around roots. Iroh let me choose the pace.

“You trust me with the road,” I said.

“I trust you to tell me when the road is unsafe.”

“That is different.”

“It is.”

“You could trust me more.”

Iroh smiled. “I could.”

“Will you?”

“I am.”

The answer was enough.

At sunset, the forest opened onto a valley full of wildflowers. I stopped the cart. Iroh climbed down.

“This is beautiful,” I said.

“It is.”

“You knew it was here.”

“I hoped.”

He took my hand. The two of I walked into the flowers, leaving the cart behind.

Iroh kissed me beneath the evening sky. There was no storm, no argument, no urgent decision. Only the quiet pleasure of finding something beautiful after difficulty.

When I returned to the cart, he tucked a small flower behind my ear.

“You are showing off,” I said.

“I am making a memory.”

I kept the flower until it dried.

When the night grew colder, I returned to the cart and built a small fire. Iroh wrapped the spare blanket around my shoulders. I protested that he was giving I all the warmth.

“I have firebending,” he said.

“That is not a substitute for a blanket.”

“It is a very effective substitute.”

“You are not allowed to set yourself on fire for romance.”

“I had not planned to.”

“Good.”

He sat beside I, close enough that my arms touched.

“You are worried about my safety,” he said.

“You are traveling through a politically unstable region with a cart full of tea.”

“A dangerous combination.”

“You say that like it is funny.”

“It is a little funny.”

“You are impossible.”

“You have said this before.”

“I am consistent.”

“A valuable quality.”

The fire snapped. Iroh looked at the flower in my notebook.

“You kept it,” he said.

“It is evidence.”

“Of what?”

“That you can find something beautiful after a difficult day.”

He touched the page. “You are learning to keep the right evidence.”

I leaned into him. The night settled around the camp. Neither of I hurried toward sleep.

The road could wait until sunrise.

I was not in a hurry.

The flowers waited in the notebook, the cart waited on the road, and Iroh waited beside I.

Together, I watched night arrive.

The flowers kept their color in the fading light.

Iroh placed one beside my notebook before I returned to the cart.
